h1: Olive Oil vs Sunflower Oil: Which One to Reach For
excerpt: Sunflower oil and olive oil sit at opposite ends of the same shelf: one is bred to disappear into a dish, the other is pressed to be tasted. This is a plain comparison for the pan, not a verdict on which is better.
keyTakeaway: Sunflower oil is neutral and takes more heat before it smokes, which suits a hard fry. Extra virgin olive oil carries its own fruity or peppery flavour and suits a raw drizzle or a moderate sauté rather than a long deep-fry. The price gap tracks how each is made, not a quality claim either way.

intro: Sunflower oil and olive oil turn up in the same Malaysian kitchen for different reasons, and the price tag on each is the first clue: one bottle costs a few ringgit, the other several times more for the same size.
This is a comparison for deciding which to reach for: flavour, how each behaves in a hot pan, what each suits, and price per use.

blocks.text: Refined sunflower oil is bred for a mild, almost nonexistent flavour, and that neutrality is the whole point: it lets a curry paste or a fried egg taste of itself and nothing else. Extra virgin olive oil is pressed straight from the fruit, so it carries its own grassy, peppery or fruity character into whatever it touches.

That is why sunflower oil disappears into a dish rather than shaping it. A peppery extra virgin can carry a plain dish on its own, but can just as easily overwhelm something already crowded with flavour.

Refined sunflower oil takes more heat before it starts to smoke than extra virgin olive oil does. Its figure sits at roughly 225°C against extra virgin's 190 to 210°C, both set out in full on [the olive oil smoke point guide](blog/olive-oil-smoke-point-what-heat-it-can-take) rather than repeated here.
That gap has nothing to do with which oil is better. Sunflower oil is processed to strip out the compounds that break down first, raising the ceiling and flattening the flavour in the same step.

sections.heading: What each oil suits in the kitchen

blocks.text: Sunflower oil's higher ceiling and quiet flavour suit sustained high heat: a proper deep-fry, a hard wok flame, or anything cooked past the point where extra virgin olive oil starts to smoke. Extra virgin suits a raw finish, a dressing, or a moderate sauté where its own flavour is meant to show.

items: **Sunflower oil** for deep-frying, a hard wok flame, or any dish that should taste only of itself.

**Extra virgin olive oil** for a raw drizzle, a dressing, or tumis at a moderate flame — see [how to cook with olive oil in a Malaysian kitchen](blog/how-to-cook-with-olive-oil-in-a-malaysian-kitchen).
Neither is a one-for-one swap for the other; each does a different job in the same kitchen.

sections.heading: Use this for that: a quick reference

blocks.text: Most kitchens keep both, and the choice on any given day comes down to whether the fat needs to survive a hard flame or carry its own flavour raw onto the plate once cooking is done.

blocks.text: Sunflower oil is a commodity crop oil, extracted from seed at scale and refined for a long shelf life — a process built for volume. Extra virgin olive oil is cold-pressed from fruit, with a lower yield and no refining step, which is the real source of the gap on the shelf.

Extra virgin olive oil is normally poured in small amounts — a drizzle, a tablespoon for tumis — so a bottle stretches further than its sticker price suggests. Sizes and pricing for Arabian Village's cold-pressed extra virgin sit on [the products page](products) rather than a fixed figure here.

Sunflower oil is usually cheaper and used more freely for deep-frying, so the two rarely compete for the same job. In Malaysia, Arabian Village's extra virgin comes only from [Berkat Madinah Store's two branches, its Shopee counter and its TikTok Shop](shop).

Reach for sunflower oil when the dish needs sustained high heat and no flavour of its own, and for extra virgin olive oil when the fat should carry its own fruit and pepper into a moderate sauté, a dressing or a finished plate. Most kitchens are better off keeping both.

faqs.q: Can I use olive oil instead of sunflower oil for deep-frying?
faqs.a: Extra virgin olive oil can be shallow-fried, but its 190–210°C range sits below refined sunflower oil's roughly 225°C, so a long deep-fry suits sunflower oil better, keeping olive oil for lower-heat cooking.

faqs.q: Which oil has a stronger flavour, olive oil or sunflower oil?
faqs.a: Extra virgin olive oil, by a wide margin. It is pressed from fruit and carries a grassy or peppery character, while refined sunflower oil is processed specifically to taste of almost nothing.

faqs.q: Why is olive oil so much more expensive than sunflower oil?
faqs.a: Different crop and different process: sunflower oil is extracted from seed at scale, while good extra virgin olive oil is cold-pressed from fruit with a lower yield. Neither price reflects which oil suits a given dish better.

faqs.q: Is sunflower oil healthier than olive oil?
faqs.a: That question belongs to a doctor or dietitian, not a kitchen comparison. This article covers flavour, smoke behaviour, what each suits and price per use.

faqs.q: What is sunflower oil's smoke point compared to olive oil's?
faqs.a: Refined sunflower oil sits at roughly 225°C. Extra virgin olive oil sits at roughly 190 to 210°C, set out in full on the site's smoke point guide rather than repeated here.

faqs.q: Does sunflower oil work for a salad dressing the way olive oil does?
faqs.a: It works, but it will not do the same job. A dressing built on extra virgin olive oil borrows its fruit and pepper as part of the flavour; sunflower oil leaves a dressing tasting mostly of the acid and salt.
